claims.evidence: This claim is supported by auxin transport measurements shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claims.claim: PIN1 S4A shows an identical behavior to wild type PIN1 in BFA sensitivity experiments.
claims.source: Since PIN1 S4A showed an identical behavior to wild type PIN1 in these experiments, we concluded that changes in PIN1 polarity, PIN1 trafficking or PIN1 abundance at the plasma membrane may not be causal for the observed differences in basipetal auxin transport.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Changes in PIN1 polarity, PIN1 trafficking or PIN1 abundance at the plasma membrane may not be causal for the observed differences in basipetal auxin transport in PIN1 S4A.
claims.source: Since PIN1 S4A showed an identical behavior to wild type PIN1 in these experiments, we concluded that changes in PIN1 polarity, PIN1 trafficking or PIN1 abundance at the plasma membrane may not be causal for the observed differences in basipetal auxin transport.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the BFA sensitivity and localization experiments.

claims.claim: The phototropism defect of the pin347 mutant is only partially complemented by the PIN3 S4A S5A transgene.
claims.source: When we measured the ability of wild type PIN3 and mutant PIN3 S4A S5A to complement the pin347 mutant when expressed from a PIN3 promoter fragment, we found that the phototropism defect of the pin347 mutant was only partially complemented by the PIN3 S4A S5A transgene while it was fully complemented by wild type PIN3 (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by phototropism measurements shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: The phototropism defect of the pin347 mutant is fully complemented by wild type PIN3.
claims.source: When we measured the ability of wild type PIN3 and mutant PIN3 S4A S5A to complement the pin347 mutant when expressed from a PIN3 promoter fragment, we found that the phototropism defect of the pin347 mutant was only partially complemented by the PIN3 S4A S5A transgene while it was fully complemented by wild type PIN3 (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by phototropism measurements shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: D6PK-dependent PIN3 S4 and S5 phosphorylations are required for efficient basipetal auxin transport in the hypocotyls of dark-grown seedlings.
claims.source: This finding was in line with the hypothesis that D6PK-dependent PIN3 S4 and S5 phosphorylations are required for efficient basipetal auxin transport in the hypocotyls of dark-grown seedlings, which is a prerequisite for efficient hypocotyl bending.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the partial complementation of the phototropism defect by PIN3 S4A S5A.

claims.claim: The mutation of the PIN3 S1–S3 phosphosites fully impairs the ability of the PIN3 transgene to complement the pin347 mutation.
claims.source: Consistent with the predominant role of the PID phosphosite phosphorylation at S1–S3, we found that the mutation of the PIN3 S1–S3 phosphosites as well as mutation of all five PIN3 phosphosites, S1–S5, fully impaired the ability of the PIN3 transgene to complement the pin347 mutation (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by phototropism measurements shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: The mutation of all five PIN3 phosphosites, S1–S5, fully impairs the ability of the PIN3 transgene to complement the pin347 mutation.
claims.source: Consistent with the predominant role of the PID phosphosite phosphorylation at S1–S3, we found that the mutation of the PIN3 S1–S3 phosphosites as well as mutation of all five PIN3 phosphosites, S1–S5, fully impaired the ability of the PIN3 transgene to complement the pin347 mutation (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by phototropism measurements shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: The novel phosphosites, PIN3 S4 and S5, are required for full PIN3 activity, most likely by interfering primarily with basipetal auxin transport in the hypocotyls of dark-grown seedlings.
claims.source: In summary, this experiment supported the conclusion that the novel phosphosites, PIN3 S4 and S5, are required for full PIN3 activity, most likely by interfering primarily with basipetal auxin transport in the hypocotyls of dark-grown seedlings.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the phototropism complementation experiments.

claims.claim: Phosphorylation at PIN1 S4 is strongly reduced in the d6pk012 triple mutant.
claims.source: In these experiments, we detected a strong reduction in the in vivo abundance of the PIN1 S4 as well as PIN3 S4 phosphorylations that increased with increasing d6pk mutant complexity (Figure 7A,B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by SRM analysis data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Phosphorylation at PIN3 S4 is strongly reduced in the d6pk012 triple mutant.
claims.source: In these experiments, we detected a strong reduction in the in vivo abundance of the PIN1 S4 as well as PIN3 S4 phosphorylations that increased with increasing d6pk mutant complexity (Figure 7A,B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by SRM analysis data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: The decrease in S4 phosphorylation cannot be explained by changes in the overall abundance of PIN proteins.
claims.source: This decrease in S4 phosphorylation could not be explained by changes in the overall abundance of PIN proteins as shown by quantitative SRM analyses of the unphosphorylated PIN1 and PIN3 S4 peptides and analyses of internal control peptides (Figure 7A,B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by SRM analysis data shown in Figure 7A and 7B.

claims.claim: Introducing a D6PK transgene expressing D6PK under control of a D6PK promoter fragment rescues the PIN1 and PIN3 S4 phosphorylation defects.
claims.source: Furthermore, introducing a D6PK transgene expressing D6PK under control of a D6PK promoter fragment rescued the PIN1 and PIN3 S4 phosphorylation defects (Figure 7—figure supplements 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by SRM analysis data shown in Figure 7—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claims.claim: The abundance of phosphorylation at PIN3 S5 is as strongly reduced in the d6pk012 triple mutant as observed for the S4 site.
claims.source: We also examined phosphorylation at PIN3 S5 using the same methodology and observed that the abundance of phosphorylation at these sites was as strongly reduced in the d6pk012 triple mutant as observed for the S4 site.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by SRM analysis data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The phosphorylation defect at PIN3 S5 is rescued by a D6PK transgene.
claims.source: Again, the phosphorylation defect could not be explained by changes in PIN3 abundance and was rescued by a D6PK transgene as described above (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by SRM analysis data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The observed decreases in PIN1 and PIN3 phosphorylation are in good agreement with the reductions in auxin transport detected in the same tissue of d6pk mutants.
claims.source: Most importantly, the observed decreases in PIN1 and PIN3 phosphorylation were in good agreement with the reductions in auxin transport that we had detected in the same tissue of d6pk mutants (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of the phosphorylation data with the auxin transport data.

claims.claim: D6PKs are the major kinases targeting PIN1 S4, PIN3 S4, and PIN3 S5 in Arabidopsis inflorescence stems.
claims.source: We therefore concluded that D6PKs are the major kinases targeting PIN1 S4, PIN3 S4, and PIN3 S5 in Arabidopsis inflorescence stems and that the reduced phosphorylation at these sites may be causal for the reduced auxin transport of d6pk mutants in this tissue.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SRM analysis data.

claims.claim: The reduced phosphorylation at PIN1 S4, PIN3 S4, and PIN3 S5 may be causal for the reduced auxin transport of d6pk mutants in inflorescence stems.
claims.source: We therefore concluded that D6PKs are the major kinases targeting PIN1 S4, PIN3 S4, and PIN3 S5 in Arabidopsis inflorescence stems and that the reduced phosphorylation at these sites may be causal for the reduced auxin transport of d6pk mutants in this tissue.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SRM analysis and auxin transport data.

claims.claim: PID and WAG2 are able to activate PIN1-mediated auxin efflux in oocytes.
claims.source: Interestingly, PID and WAG2 but not phot1 or UCN were able to activate PIN1-mediated auxin efflux (Figure 8A,B, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by oocyte auxin efflux assay data shown in Figure 8A, 8B, and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: phot1 and UCN are not able to activate PIN1-mediated auxin efflux in oocytes.
claims.source: Interestingly, PID and WAG2 but not phot1 or UCN were able to activate PIN1-mediated auxin efflux (Figure 8A,B, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by oocyte auxin efflux assay data shown in Figure 8A and 8B.

claims.claim: PID and WAG2 have a role in PIN activation besides their previously reported role in the control of PIN polarity.
claims.source: We thus concluded that PID and WAG2 have a role in PIN activation besides their previously reported role in the control of PIN polarity (Friml et al., 2004; Dhonukshe et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the oocyte auxin efflux assay data.

claims.claim: The PIN1 S1A S2A S3A mutant is less efficiently activated by PID than by D6PK.
claims.source: Indeed, we found, in agreement with the in vitro data, that the PIN1 S1A S2A S3A mutant was less efficiently activated by PID than by D6PK (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by oocyte auxin efflux assay data shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: The PIN1 S4A mutation does not significantly affect activation by PID.
claims.source: Inversely, the PIN1 S4A mutation that strongly affected activation by D6PK did not significantly affect activation by PID.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by oocyte auxin efflux assay data shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: Mutation of all four PIN1 phosphosites, PIN1 S1A–S4A, results in the strongest impairment of PIN1 activation by PID.
claims.source: Again, mutation of all four PIN1 phosphosites, PIN1 S1A–S4A, resulted in the strongest impairment of PIN1 activation by PID (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by oocyte auxin efflux assay data shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: Neither pid nor wag1 wag2 mutants show a clear reduction in PIN S4 phosphorylation.
claims.source: However, in contrast to the strong defects in PIN S4 phosphorylation that we observed in the d6pk mutants, neither pid nor wag1 wag2 mutants showed a clear reduction in PIN phosphorylation at the S4 phosphosite suggesting that PID and WAG1/WAG2 do not contribute to PIN S4 phosphorylation in this tissue.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by SRM analysis data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2 and Figure 8—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: PID and WAG1/WAG2 do not contribute to PIN S4 phosphorylation in inflorescence stems.
claims.source: However, in contrast to the strong defects in PIN S4 phosphorylation that we observed in the d6pk mutants, neither pid nor wag1 wag2 mutants showed a clear reduction in PIN phosphorylation at the S4 phosphosite suggesting that PID and WAG1/WAG2 do not contribute to PIN S4 phosphorylation in this tissue.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SRM analysis data.

claims.claim: The phosphorylation at the S1 phosphosites is not affected when comparing the d6pk012 mutant with the d6pk012 mutant expressing a complementing D6PK transgene.
claims.source: Our analysis of PIN1 and PIN3 S1 phosphorylations, however, showed that the phosphorylation at the S1 phosphosites was not affected when comparing the d6pk012 mutant with the d6pk012 mutant expressing a complementing D6PK transgene suggesting that D6PK does not contribute to the phosphorylation of S1 in vivo (Figure 8—figure supplements 4 and 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by SRM analysis data shown in Figure 8—figure supplements 4 and 5.

claims.claim: D6PK does not contribute to the phosphorylation of S1 in vivo.
claims.source: Our analysis of PIN1 and PIN3 S1 phosphorylations, however, showed that the phosphorylation at the S1 phosphosites was not affected when comparing the d6pk012 mutant with the d6pk012 mutant expressing a complementing D6PK transgene suggesting that D6PK does not contribute to the phosphorylation of S1 in vivo (Figure 8—figure supplements 4 and 5).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SRM analysis data.

claims.claim: D6PK and PID cannot functionally replace each other when expressed from the promoter of the respective other gene.
claims.source: These experiments demonstrated that D6PK and PID cannot functionally replace each other when expressed from the promoter of the respective other gene (Figure 9).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genetic complementation experiments shown in Figure 9.

claims.claim: The expression of PID from a PID promoter fragment is sufficient to complement the phenotypes of a pid mutant.
claims.source: Whereas the expression of PID from a PID promoter fragment was sufficient to complement the phenotypes of a pid mutant, the expression of D6PK under control of the PID promoter fragment failed to complement pid (Figure 9A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genetic complementation experiments shown in Figure 9A.

claims.claim: The expression of D6PK under control of the PID promoter fragment fails to complement pid.
claims.source: Whereas the expression of PID from a PID promoter fragment was sufficient to complement the phenotypes of a pid mutant, the expression of D6PK under control of the PID promoter fragment failed to complement pid (Figure 9A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genetic complementation experiments shown in Figure 9A.

claims.claim: D6PK expression from a D6PK promoter fragment is sufficient to complement the d6pk012 mutant.
claims.source: Inversely, D6PK but not PID expression from a D6PK promoter fragment was sufficient to complement the d6pk012 mutant (Figure 9B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genetic complementation experiments shown in Figure 9B.

claims.claim: PID expression from a D6PK promoter fragment is not sufficient to complement the d6pk012 mutant.
claims.source: Inversely, D6PK but not PID expression from a D6PK promoter fragment was sufficient to complement the d6pk012 mutant (Figure 9B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genetic complementation experiments shown in Figure 9B.

claims.claim: D6PK and PID/WAGs are functionally divergent.
claims.source: In summary, these genetic experiments supported our conclusion that D6PK and PID/WAGs are functionally divergent and these findings and conclusions are in line with previous observations on the differential effects of these two kinases in PIN polarity control (Dhonukshe et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic complementation experiments.

claims.claim: Differential phosphosite preferences may be the basis of the distinct roles of D6PK and PID/WAGs in the control of PIN polarity and plant growth control.
claims.source: These differential phosophosite preferences as detected in in vitro as well as in vivo phosphosite analyses may be the basis of the distinct roles of the two kinases in the control of PIN polarity and plant growth control.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about the molecular basis of functional differences.

claims.claim: Concentration-, time- and D6PK-dependent increases in the phosphorylation of PIN1 S4, PIN3 S4 and PIN3 S5 occur already 15 min after auxin application.
claims.source: In these analyses, we detected concentration-, time- and D6PK-dependent increases in the phosphorylation of PIN1 S4, PIN3 S4 and PIN3 S5 already 15 min after auxin application (Figure 10A,B, Figure 10—figure supplements 1–4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by SRM analysis data shown in Figure 10 and related supplements.

claims.claim: Only marginal increases in PIN phosphorylation at S4 and S5 are observed in the phosphorylation deficient d6pk012 mutant after auxin treatment.
claims.source: While these increases were clearly observed in the wild type, only marginal increases in PIN phosphorylation at these sites were observed in the phosphorylation deficient d6pk012 mutant.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by SRM analysis data shown in Figure 10 and related supplements.

claims.claim: Phosphorylation at the preferential PID target site S1 is neither strongly impaired in d6pk012 mutants nor clearly induced by auxin.
claims.source: At the same time, phosphorylation at the preferential PID target site S1 was neither strongly impaired in d6pk012 mutants when compared to a d6pk012 mutant expressing a complementing D6PK transgene nor clearly induced by auxin (Figure 8—figure supplements 4 and 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by SRM analysis data shown in Figure 8—figure supplements 4 and 5.

claims.claim: Increased phosphorylation at S4 and S5 is detected in the auxin-overproducing yucca mutant.
claims.source: Furthermore, in agreement with an auxin-dependent control of PIN phosphorylation at S4 and S5, we detected increased phosphorylation at S4 and S5 in the auxin-overproducing yucca mutant (Figure 10A,B, Figure 10—figure supplements 1–4; Zhao et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by SRM analysis data shown in Figure 10 and related supplements.

claims.claim: The relative increases in phosphosite phosphorylations in yucca exceed the increases in overall PIN abundance.
claims.source: Although the analyses of the control peptides showed that there is also an overall increase in PIN abundance in yucca, the relative increases in phosphosite phosphorylations exceeded the increases in overall PIN abundance suggesting that PIN phosphorylation is activated in this mutant when compared to the wild type.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by SRM analysis data shown in Figure 10 and related supplements.

claims.claim: PIN phosphorylation is activated in the yucca mutant when compared to the wild type.
claims.source: Although the analyses of the control peptides showed that there is also an overall increase in PIN abundance in yucca, the relative increases in phosphosite phosphorylations exceeded the increases in overall PIN abundance suggesting that PIN phosphorylation is activated in this mutant when compared to the wild type.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SRM analysis data.

claims.claim: PIN1 S4 phosphorylation is strongly decreased minutes after BFA treatment when D6PK has become dissociated from the plasma membrane.
claims.source: Importantly, we found that PIN1 S4 phosphorylation was strongly decreased already minutes after BFA treatment when D6PK had become dissociated from the plasma membrane (Figure 11).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining and confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 11.

claims.claim: PIN1 S4 phosphorylation depends on the presence of D6PK or other BFA-sensitive protein kinases at the plasma membrane.
claims.source: Thus, PIN1 S4 phosphorylation depended on the presence of D6PK or other BFA-sensitive protein kinases at the plasma membrane.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the BFA treatment experiments.

claims.claim: d6pk mutants are impaired in basipetal auxin transport in inflorescence stems.
claims.source: In this study, we examined the functional roles of the D6PK protein kinases in PIN phosphorylation and auxin transport activation. We showed that d6pk mutants are impaired in basipetal auxin transport in inflorescence stems
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by auxin transport measurements presented in the study.

claims.claim: The decreases in auxin transport in inflorescence stems are not the consequence of changes in PIN abundance.
claims.source: Furthermore, we could rule out that the decreases in auxin transport as measured in inflorescence stems are the consequence of changes in PIN abundance as demonstrated using confocal imaging, immunoblotting, and SRM analyses of PIN proteins.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging, immunoblotting, and SRM analyses.

claims.claim: D6PK-dependent PIN activation is dependent on specific phosphosites in PIN1 and PIN3.
claims.source: We furthermore demonstrated that D6PK-dependent PIN activation was dependent on specific phosphosites in PIN1 and PIN3.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by oocyte auxin efflux assays with phosphosite mutants.

claims.claim: D6PKs are major regulators of PIN-mediated auxin transport in inflorescence stems.
claims.source: Taken together, all our findings support the conclusion that D6PKs are major regulators of PIN-mediated auxin transport in inflorescence stems.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental data.

claims.claim: d6pk mutant phenotypes such as gravitropism defects in the root, negative gravitropism defects in the hypocotyl, phototropism defects in the hypocotyl and defects in lateral root initiation are also the consequence of reduced auxin transport activity of PINs.
claims.source: Since d6pk mutants have a number of phenotypes such as gravitropism defects in the root, negative gravitropism defects in the hypocotyl, phototropism defects in the hypocotyl as well as defects in lateral root initiation (Zourelidou et al., 2009; Willige et al., 2013; Barbosa et al., 2014), we are tempted to speculate that these other d6pk mutant phenotypes are also the consequence of reduced auxin transport activity of PINs in the absence of the PIN-activating D6PK kinases.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about the cause of d6pk mutant phenotypes.

claims.claim: PIN1 S4 as well as PIN3 S4 and S5 are major target sites for D6PK.
claims.source: The detailed analysis of the S1–S5 phosphosites in in vitro phosphorylation experiments and in oocyte auxin transport experiments revealed that PIN1 S4 as well as PIN3 S4 and S5 are major target sites for D6PK.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from in vitro phosphorylation and oocyte auxin transport experiments.

claims.claim: The preferential D6PK phosphosites S4 and S5 are not conserved in PIN2.
claims.source: Interestingly, the preferential D6PK phosphosites S4 and S5 are not conserved in PIN2 and it is striking that the respective domains in PIN2 carry small insertions when compared to the other PIN proteins.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data.

claims.claim: The activation of PINs by phosphorylation may be regulated by the presence and abundance of activating kinases such as D6PK but also by the availability and conservation of phosphosites in their PIN targets.
claims.source: Thus, the activation of PINs by phosphorylation may be regulated by the presence and abundance of activating kinases such as D6PK but also by the availability and conservation of phosphosites in their PIN targets.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the phosphosite conservation analysis.

claims.claim: PINs must have other phosphosites that are targeted by D6PK besides S4 and S5.
claims.source: Besides S4 and S5, PINs must have other phosphosites that are targeted by D6PK since auxin transport defects in pin mutants expressing the respective PIN S4A and S5A mutant variants are partially complemented and not as severe as those observed in the d6pk012 loss-of-function mutants.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the partial complementation of pin mutants by S4A and S5A variants.

claims.claim: D6PK has a preference for the S4 and S5 sites in PIN1 and PIN3.
claims.source: Whereas D6PK appeared to have a preference for the S4 and S5 sites in PIN1 and PIN3, PID preferentially phosphorylated the previously identified S1–S3 phosphosites.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from in vitro phosphorylation and mass spectrometry data.

claims.claim: PID preferentially phosphorylates the S1–S3 phosphosites.
claims.source: Whereas D6PK appeared to have a preference for the S4 and S5 sites in PIN1 and PIN3, PID preferentially phosphorylated the previously identified S1–S3 phosphosites.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from in vitro phosphorylation and mass spectrometry data.

claims.claim: S1–S3 are highly related to each other and also highly conserved among all five plasma membrane-resident PIN auxin efflux carriers including PIN2.
claims.source: S1–S3 are highly related to each other and also highly conserved among all five plasma membrane-resident PIN auxin efflux carriers including PIN2.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data.

claims.claim: The phosphorylation of S1–S3 contributes to full PIN phosphorylation and activation by D6PK.
claims.source: Although D6PK had a preference for S4 and S5 phosphorylation, our in vitro phosphorylation experiments as well as the auxin transport experiments in oocytes further suggested that the phosphorylation of S1–S3 also contributes to full PIN phosphorylation and activation by D6PK.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from in vitro phosphorylation and oocyte auxin transport experiments.

claims.claim: Full impairment of phosphorylation and activation by PID can only be achieved after S4 mutation.
claims.source: Whereas PID phosphorylation and activation of PIN1 was strongly impaired when S1–S3 were mutated, full impairment of phosphorylation and activation could only be achieved after S4 mutation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from in vitro phosphorylation and oocyte auxin transport experiments.

claims.claim: PIN1 S4 is not the only phosphosite required for D6PK-dependent PIN1 activation and basipetal auxin transport.
claims.source: The partial complementation of the pin1 auxin transport defect indicates that PIN1 S4 is not the only phosphosite required for D6PK-dependent PIN1 activation and basipetal auxin transport.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the partial complementation of pin1 by PIN1 S4A.

claims.claim: The essential phosphosites required for PID-dependent PIN activation and PIN polarity changes are retained in PIN1 S4A.
claims.source: As shown in the in vitro phosphorylation experiment as well as in the oocyte auxin transport experiment, the PIN1 S4A mutant variant is neither strongly impaired in its phosphorylation by PID nor in its activation by PID. Thus, the essential phosphosites required for PID-dependent PIN activation and PIN polarity changes are retained in PIN1 S4A.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from in vitro phosphorylation and oocyte auxin transport experiments.

claims.claim: Phosphorylation at S4 and S5 is important for PIN3 activation but other phosphosites, such as S1–S3, may also be targeted by D6PK.
claims.source: Our observation that the PIN3 S4A S5A transgene could only partially rescue the pin347 triple mutant phenotype supports the notion that phosphorylation at these sites is important for PIN3 activation but suggests further that other phosphosites, such as S1–S3, may also be targeted by D6PK.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the partial complementation of pin347 by PIN3 S4A S5A.

claims.claim: PIN phosphorylation led to a direct activation of auxin efflux in oocytes.
claims.source: In our experiments, PIN phosphorylation led to a direct activation of auxin efflux in oocytes.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by oocyte auxin efflux assay data.

claims.claim: The primary function of PIN phosphorylation is the activation of auxin transport.
claims.source: The analysis of auxin transport in Arabidopsis inflorescence stems suggested that this might indeed be the primary function of this modification since auxin transport was strongly impaired in d6pk loss-of-function mutants while PIN abundance at the plasma membrane was not altered.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from auxin transport and PIN abundance data.

claims.claim: PIN phosphorylation may have other regulatory roles such as control of PIN polarity by PID or WAG-dependent phosphorylation.
claims.source: This observation does, however, not rule out that PIN phosphorylation has other regulatory roles such control of PIN polarity by PID or WAG-dependent phosphorylation (Friml et al., 2004; Dhonukshe et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is a statement acknowledging other known functions of PIN phosphorylation.

claims.claim: Changes in PIN polarity are observed after PID or WAG2 overexpression but not after D6PK overexpression.
claims.source: Changes in PIN polarity as they are observed after PID or WAG2 overexpression are not observed after D6PK overexpression (Zourelidou et al., 2009; Dhonukshe et al., 2010; Barbosa et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: The differential effect of D6PK and PID/WAGs on PIN may have its molecular basis in the differential phosphosite preferences of the two kinases.
claims.source: The differential effect of D6PK and PID/WAGs on PIN may have its molecular basis in the differential phosphosite preferences of the two kinases.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about the molecular basis of functional differences.

claims.claim: The phosphorylation activity of both D6PK and PID/WAGs is antagonistically regulated by phosphatases.
claims.source: Common to both kinases seems, however, the fact that their phosphorylation activity is antagonistically regulated by phosphatases.
claims.evidence: This is a statement based on observations about phosphatase regulation.

claims.claim: The phenotypic effects of PID can be antagonized by PP2A phosphatases.
claims.source: While the phenotypic effects of PID can be antagonized by PP2A phosphatases (Michniewicz et al., 2007), removal of the D6PK from the plasma membrane through BFA treatment resulted in an almost immediate decrease in PIN1 phosphorylation.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Removal of D6PK from the plasma membrane through BFA treatment results in an almost immediate decrease in PIN1 phosphorylation.
claims.source: While the phenotypic effects of PID can be antagonized by PP2A phosphatases (Michniewicz et al., 2007), removal of the D6PK from the plasma membrane through BFA treatment resulted in an almost immediate decrease in PIN1 phosphorylation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by BFA treatment experiments.

claims.claim: D6PK-dependent PIN phosphorylation is antagonized by phosphatases.
claims.source: Thus, it can be speculated that also D6PK-dependent PIN phosphorylation is antagonized by phosphatases, the identities of which remain to be determined.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the rapid dephosphorylation observed after BFA treatment.

claims.claim: PIN1 and PIN3 phosphorylation is controlled by the presence of D6PK at the plasma membrane.
claims.source: Our data also suggest that PIN1 and PIN3 phosphorylation is not only controlled by the presence of D6PK at the plasma membrane but also by auxin itself.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from BFA treatment experiments.

claims.claim: PIN1 and PIN3 phosphorylation is controlled by auxin.
claims.source: Our data also suggest that PIN1 and PIN3 phosphorylation is not only controlled by the presence of D6PK at the plasma membrane but also by auxin itself.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from auxin treatment experiments.

claims.claim: PIN1 S4 as well as PIN3 S4 and S5 phosphorylation increases in response to auxin treatment in the wild type.
claims.source: Using quantitative SRM analyses, we could show that PIN1 S4 as well as PIN3 S4 and S5 phosphorylation increases in response to auxin treatment in the wild type.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by SRM analysis data.

claims.claim: The loss of phosphorylation at the preferential D6PK phosphosites in d6pk012 mutants cannot be compensated by auxin application.
claims.source: In the d6pk012 mutant, the loss of phosphorylation at these preferential D6PK phosphosites could not be compensated by auxin application suggesting that these auxin-dependent phosphorylations are D6PK-dependent and may be mediated either directly by D6PK or by D6PK acting as an indirect auxiliary factor.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by SRM analysis data.

claims.claim: Auxin-dependent phosphorylations at S4 and S5 are D6PK-dependent and may be mediated either directly by D6PK or by D6PK acting as an indirect auxiliary factor.
claims.source: In the d6pk012 mutant, the loss of phosphorylation at these preferential D6PK phosphosites could not be compensated by auxin application suggesting that these auxin-dependent phosphorylations are D6PK-dependent and may be mediated either directly by D6PK or by D6PK acting as an indirect auxiliary factor.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the auxin treatment experiments in d6pk012 mutants.

claims.claim: The auxin-dependent increases in PIN phosphorylation may be the consequence of the inhibitory effects of auxin on PIN endocytosis.
claims.source: Theoretically, it could be envisioned that the auxin-dependent increases in PIN phosphorylation are the consequence of the previously reported inhibitory effects of auxin on PIN endocytosis (Paciorek et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about a possible mechanism.

claims.claim: PIN phosphorylating kinases would encounter their PIN targets for a longer period of time if auxin inhibits PIN endocytosis, thereby increasing the chances for phosphorylation.

claims.claim: PIN-mediated auxin efflux requires activation by PIN phosphorylating kinases such as D6PK and PID/WAGs.
claims.source: In summary, our study provides evidence that PIN-mediated auxin efflux requires activation by PIN phosphorylating kinases such as D6PK and PID/WAGs.

claims.source: Several of our findings point at a differential biochemical activity of these two AGCVIII kinase representatives on PINs that may explain their differential effects in controlling PIN polarity, auxin transport, and plant growth.

claims.claim: The activation of PINs by D6PKs and PID/WAGs is a crucial component of the control of auxin transport.
claims.source: It is our view that the activation of PINs by D6PKs and PID/WAGs is a crucial component of the control of auxin transport that must be taken into account to understand auxin transport within the plant and to ultimately understand plant growth.
claims.evidence: This is a concluding statement about the importance of the findings.

results.result: D6PKs are essential for basipetal auxin transport in Arabidopsis inflorescence stems. The d6pk012 triple mutant shows auxin transport defects as severe as pin1 mutants, D6PKs are coexpressed with PINs in stems, and both D6PK and PIN1 localize to the basal plasma membrane in cells with high auxin levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C50 are well-supported by auxin transport measurements (Figure 1), GUS reporter data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and confocal microscopy showing colocalization (Figure 1—figure supplement 2). The statistical analysis confirms significant differences between genotypes, and the d6pk012 triple mutant shows transport defects comparable to pin1 mutants.

results.result: D6PK directly activates PIN-mediated auxin efflux in Xenopus oocytes. PIN1 and PIN3 alone show no measurable auxin efflux above background, but co-expression with active D6PK results in significant, kinase activity-dependent activation of auxin efflux, correlated with appearance of high molecular weight PIN bands indicating phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C55 are strongly supported by oocyte auxin efflux assays (Figure 2C-F) and immunoblot data (Figure 2B) showing phosphorylation-dependent activation. The kinase-dead D6PK variant fails to activate auxin efflux, providing critical negative control evidence. This is a novel heterologous system demonstrating direct PIN activation.

results.result: D6PK phosphorylates PINs at specific sites including two novel phosphosites S4 and S5. Mass spectrometry identified S4 and S5 as conserved phosphosites in PIN1, PIN3, PIN4, and PIN7, but not in PIN2. S1-S3 are conserved in all tested PINs. In vitro phosphorylation experiments with synthetic peptides confirmed D6PK can phosphorylate S4 and S5 sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C63 are well-supported by mass spectrometry data (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—source data 1) and in vitro phosphorylation experiments with synthetic peptides (Figure 3B). The sequence alignment data clearly shows differential conservation of phosphosites among PIN proteins. The identification of novel phosphosites is a significant finding.

results.result: D6PK and PID have differential phosphosite preferences in PIN1. S4 is a major phosphosite for D6PK (S4A mutation reduces phosphorylation to 40%), while S1-S3 mutations have lesser individual effects. In contrast, PID phosphorylation is not affected by S4A mutation but is strongly affected by S1A mutation.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C72 are supported by quantitative in vitro phosphorylation experiments (Figure 4A,B) showing differential effects of phosphosite mutations on D6PK vs PID phosphorylation. The quantitative data clearly demonstrate that D6PK preferentially targets S4 while PID preferentially targets S1-S3. This establishes biochemical specificity.

results.result: PIN3 S4 and S5 mutations have differential effects on phosphorylation by D6PK versus PID. PIN3 S4A S5A is still efficiently phosphorylated by PID but phosphorylation by D6PK is severely impaired (28% of wild type).
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C75 are supported by in vitro phosphorylation data (Figure 4C,D) showing differential effects of S4A S5A mutations on D6PK versus PID phosphorylation of PIN3. This extends the differential phosphosite preference finding from PIN1 to PIN3.

results.result: Specific phosphosites are required for D6PK-dependent PIN activation in oocytes. PIN1 S4A is significantly impaired in auxin efflux activation by D6PK, and the defect is enhanced when combined with S1A S2A S3A mutations. PIN3 S4A S5A shows reduced responsiveness to D6PK compared to wild type PIN3.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C79 are supported by oocyte auxin efflux assays with phosphosite mutants (Figure 5A-C). The functional data correlate well with the in vitro phosphorylation data, demonstrating that the identified phosphosites are functionally important for PIN activation. The graded effects of different mutations provide insight into relative importance of sites.

results.result: PIN1 D215S mutation does not affect auxin efflux activation compared to wild type PIN1 in oocytes.
results.evaluation: Claim C80 is supported by oocyte auxin efflux data (Figure 5D) showing indistinguishable behavior between wild type PIN1 and PIN1 D215S. This negative result is important for ruling out D215 as a functional phosphomimic of S5 in PIN1.

results.result: PIN1 S4 is important for D6PK-dependent auxin transport in planta but not for PID-dependent inflorescence development. PIN1 S4A partially rescues auxin transport defects in pin1 mutants but fully complements the PID-dependent inflorescence differentiation defect. PIN1 S4A shows identical behavior to wild type in BFA sensitivity experiments, suggesting the transport defect is not due to altered polarity or trafficking.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C85 are supported by auxin transport measurements in inflorescence stems (Figure 6A,B), phenotypic analysis (Figure 6C,D), and confocal microscopy of BFA-treated roots (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). The partial rescue of transport but full rescue of development phenotype provides strong evidence for differential roles of S4 phosphorylation in D6PK versus PID function.

results.result: PIN3 S4 and S5 are required for full PIN3 activity in phototropism, likely through effects on basipetal auxin transport. PIN3 S4A S5A only partially complements the phototropism defect of pin347 mutants, while wild type PIN3 fully complements. Mutation of S1-S3 or all five sites (S1-S5) fully impairs complementation.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C91 are supported by phototropism measurements (Figure 6E,F) showing differential complementation by wild type versus mutant PIN3 transgenes. The partial complementation by S4A S5A and complete loss of function with S1-S3 mutations is consistent with both D6PK and PID/WAG phosphorylation being required for full PIN3 function in phototropism.

results.result: D6PKs are the major kinases targeting PIN1 S4, PIN3 S4, and PIN3 S5 in Arabidopsis inflorescence stems. SRM analysis shows strong reduction in phosphorylation at these sites in d6pk mutants that increases with mutant complexity, cannot be explained by changes in PIN abundance, and is rescued by a D6PK transgene. The decreases in phosphorylation correlate with reductions in auxin transport.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C100 are strongly supported by quantitative SRM mass spectrometry data (Figure 7A,B and supplements) showing specific, D6PK-dependent phosphorylation at S4 and S5 sites in vivo. The correlation with auxin transport defects provides functional validation. This is a critical result linking in vitro phosphorylation to in vivo function.

results.result: PID and WAG2, but not phot1 or UCN, can activate PIN1-mediated auxin efflux in oocytes, indicating PID and WAG2 have a role in PIN activation beyond their known role in PIN polarity control.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C103 are supported by oocyte auxin efflux assays (Figure 8A,B, Figure 8—figure supplement 1) showing selective activation by PID and WAG2. The negative results with phot1 and UCN (with appropriate controls showing protein expression) strengthen the conclusion that PIN activation is specific to certain AGCVIII kinases.

results.result: PID shows differential phosphosite preferences compared to D6PK in oocyte activation assays. PIN1 S1A S2A S3A is less efficiently activated by PID than by D6PK, while PIN1 S4A does not significantly affect PID activation. Mutation of all four sites (S1A-S4A) results in strongest impairment of PID activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C106 are supported by oocyte auxin efflux assays with phosphosite mutants (Figure 8C). The functional data in oocytes are consistent with the in vitro phosphorylation data, confirming differential phosphosite preferences translate to differential activation requirements.

results.result: PID and WAG1/WAG2 do not contribute to PIN S4 phosphorylation in inflorescence stems, and D6PK does not contribute to S1 phosphorylation in vivo. SRM analysis shows no clear reduction in PIN S4 phosphorylation in pid or wag1 wag2 mutants, and no effect on S1 phosphorylation when comparing d6pk012 mutants with or without a complementing D6PK transgene.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C110 are supported by SRM analysis data (Figure 8—figure supplements 2-5) showing tissue-specific phosphorylation patterns. These negative results are important for establishing that the differential phosphosite preferences observed in vitro are maintained in vivo in inflorescence stems, though the limited technical ability to measure S2 and S3 is a weakness.

results.result: D6PK and PID are functionally divergent and cannot replace each other when expressed from the promoter of the other gene. PID expressed from its own promoter complements pid mutants but D6PK expressed from the PID promoter does not. Conversely, D6PK but not PID expressed from a D6PK promoter complements d6pk012 mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C116 are supported by genetic complementation experiments (Figure 9) showing reciprocal failure of cross-complementation. This provides strong genetic evidence for functional divergence, though the result could be due to expression level/pattern differences rather than purely biochemical differences. The authors acknowledge this is consistent with previous observations on differential effects in PIN polarity control.

results.result: Auxin promotes PIN phosphorylation at S4 and S5 in a D6PK-dependent manner. SRM analysis shows concentration-, time-, and D6PK-dependent increases in PIN1 S4, PIN3 S4, and PIN3 S5 phosphorylation within 15 minutes of auxin application in wild type but not in d6pk012 mutants. Increased phosphorylation is also detected in the auxin-overproducing yucca mutant, exceeding increases in overall PIN abundance.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C123 are supported by SRM analysis data (Figure 10 and supplements) showing auxin-induced phosphorylation changes. The time course, concentration dependence, and D6PK dependence provide strong evidence for auxin regulation of PIN phosphorylation. The yucca mutant data provide additional genetic support, though the interpretation is complicated by overall increases in PIN abundance.

results.result: PIN1 S4 phosphorylation depends on the presence of D6PK or other BFA-sensitive protein kinases at the plasma membrane. Immunostaining shows PIN1 S4 phosphorylation is strongly decreased within minutes after BFA treatment when D6PK has dissociated from the plasma membrane.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C125 are supported by immunostaining and confocal microscopy data (Figure 11) using a phosphosite-specific antibody. The rapid dephosphorylation after BFA treatment provides evidence for dynamic regulation of PIN phosphorylation and suggests antagonistic phosphatase activity, though the identity of the phosphatases remains unknown.

results.result: D6PKs are major regulators of PIN-mediated auxin transport in inflorescence stems. Multiple lines of evidence show d6pk mutants are impaired in basipetal auxin transport, the decreases are not due to changes in PIN abundance, and D6PK-dependent PIN activation depends on specific phosphosites.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C129 represent a synthesis of multiple experimental approaches (auxin transport assays, confocal imaging, immunoblotting, SRM analyses, oocyte assays) that collectively support the conclusion. This is a well-supported major conclusion of the paper integrating multiple lines of evidence.

results.result: Other d6pk mutant phenotypes (gravitropism defects, phototropism defects, lateral root initiation defects) may also be consequences of reduced auxin transport activity of PINs.
results.evaluation: Claim C130 is explicitly speculative and not directly tested in this study. While the hypothesis is reasonable based on the findings in inflorescence stems, it requires additional experiments in the relevant tissues to be validated. The authors appropriately present this as speculation.

results.result: PIN1 S4 and PIN3 S4/S5 are major target sites for D6PK, but other phosphosites must also be targeted. The preferential D6PK phosphosites S4 and S5 are not conserved in PIN2. The activation of PINs by phosphorylation may be regulated by both kinase presence/abundance and phosphosite availability/conservation.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C134 are supported by in vitro phosphorylation, oocyte transport, and sequence alignment data. The inference that other phosphosites must exist (C134) is reasonable based on partial complementation by S4A/S5A mutants, though the specific sites are not identified. The observation about PIN2 divergence is well-supported by sequence data.

results.result: D6PK and PID have overlapping but differential phosphosite preferences. D6PK prefers S4 and S5 sites while PID preferentially phosphorylates S1-S3. S1-S3 are highly conserved among all plasma membrane-resident PINs. Both S1-S3 and S4 contribute to full phosphorylation and activation by both kinases.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C139 synthesize findings from in vitro phosphorylation, oocyte assays, and sequence analysis. The differential preferences are well-documented, though the claim of overlapping activity (C138) is based on incomplete inhibition by single-site mutations rather than direct demonstration of phosphorylation at all sites by both kinases.

results.result: Multiple phosphosites contribute to PIN function. PIN1 S4 is not the only phosphosite required for D6PK-dependent activation and transport. The essential phosphosites for PID-dependent activation and polarity changes are retained in PIN1 S4A. For PIN3, S4 and S5 are important but S1-S3 may also be targeted by D6PK.
results.evaluation: Claims C140-C142 are supported by partial complementation data and differential effects on PID versus D6PK function. The interpretation that multiple sites contribute is well-supported, though the specific contribution of S1-S3 to D6PK function in vivo remains somewhat uncertain given the inability to measure S2 and S3 phosphorylation directly.

results.result: The primary function of PIN phosphorylation is activation of auxin transport, though it may have other regulatory roles. PIN phosphorylation led to direct activation of auxin efflux in oocytes, and auxin transport was impaired in d6pk mutants without altered PIN abundance. The differential effect of D6PK and PID/WAGs may have its molecular basis in differential phosphosite preferences.
results.evaluation: Claims C143-C147 represent interpretations and conclusions from the data. The evidence for activation as the primary function (C144) is strong in inflorescence stems but the claim doesn't rule out other functions (C145). The speculation about molecular basis (C147) is reasonable but not definitively proven. Overall well-supported as a major conclusion with appropriate caveats.

results.result: PIN phosphorylation by both D6PK and PID/WAGs is antagonistically regulated by phosphatases. PID effects can be antagonized by PP2A phosphatases, and removal of D6PK from the plasma membrane results in rapid decrease in PIN1 phosphorylation, suggesting phosphatase activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C148-C151 are partially supported. C149 is established knowledge from prior work. C150 is supported by BFA treatment data (Figure 11). C151 is a reasonable speculation based on the rapid dephosphorylation, though the specific phosphatases are not identified. The overall conclusion about phosphatase regulation is well-supported.

results.result: PIN phosphorylation is controlled by both D6PK presence at the plasma membrane and by auxin. PIN1 S4 and PIN3 S4/S5 phosphorylation increases in response to auxin treatment in wild type, and this auxin-dependent phosphorylation is D6PK-dependent and cannot be compensated in d6pk012 mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C152-C156 are supported by BFA treatment experiments and auxin treatment experiments with SRM analysis. The dual regulation by kinase localization and auxin provides a mechanism for dynamic control of PIN activity. The D6PK-dependence of auxin-induced phosphorylation is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: The mechanism of auxin-dependent PIN phosphorylation regulation may differ between tissues. Auxin promotes PIN phosphorylation in inflorescence stems but previous work showed auxin causes transient D6PK dissociation and slight decrease in PIN1 phosphorylation in roots.
results.evaluation: Claims C157-C161 attempt to reconcile apparently contradictory observations between this study and previous work. C157-C158 are speculative mechanisms. C159 cites previous work. C160 is supported by data in this study. C161 is speculation to explain the discrepancy. The tissue-specific regulation hypothesis is reasonable but not directly tested.

results.result: PIN-mediated auxin efflux requires activation by PIN phosphorylating kinases such as D6PK and PID/WAGs. These kinases have differential biochemical activity on PINs that may explain their differential effects in controlling PIN polarity, auxin transport, and plant growth. PIN activation by these kinases is a crucial component of auxin transport control.
results.evaluation: Claims C162-C165 represent the main conclusions of the paper. They are well-supported by the comprehensive set of experiments including oocyte assays, in vitro phosphorylation, in vivo phosphorylation analysis, genetic complementation, and auxin transport measurements. The differential biochemical activity is clearly demonstrated, though the mechanistic link to differential biological functions remains somewhat speculative.
